newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin defends Chechen policy against opponents.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin defends Chechen policy against opponents.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, responding to criticism of his peace moves in breakaway Chechnya, on Thursday defended his right as Russia's supreme military commander to decide on troop movements.

Yeltsin's communist and nationalist opponents in the State Duma lower house of parliament have condemned a presidential decree last Saturday ordering Russia's last two units to leave Chechnya ahead of planned regional elections.

His press spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing for Russian media that Yeltsin had sent a letter to the communist speaker of the Duma saying the president alone could rule on the stationing of troops, Interfax news agency said.
Yeltsin's foes plan an extraordinary parliamentary session on Friday to discuss the issue of troop withdrawal, which they say effectively sanctions Chechen independence.

In his letter to the speaker Gennady Seleznyov, Yeltsin tried to calm deputies' fears, saying he as president was ultimately responsible for safeguarding Russia's territorial integrity, Interfax quoted Yastrzhembsky as saying.

Yeltsin has asked Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and the secretary of the Security Council, Ivan Rybkin, to provide a written account to deputies of all recently signed documents concerning the peace process in Chechnya, Yastrzhembsky said.
The president, who is recovering from heart surgery at a sanatorium near Moscow, wants to win parliamentary support for the fragile peace process in Chechnya.
Yeltsin's decision to withdraw the last two units means that Russia has met all the rebels' demands except full independence.
The August peace accord, which halted 21 months of bloody fighting in Chechnya, deferred a final decision on the region's political status for five years.
Some deputies have threatened to try to impeach Yeltsin in Friday's debate, though this would be a long drawn-out procedure that has virtually no chance of success.
RIA news agency said some armoured vehicles left Chechnya on Thursday. Troops, who number about 6,000, will start pulling out on December 1, Interfax said on Wednesday.
Elections in Chechnya are scheduled for January 27.
